rib-cartilage-rhinoplasty.summary: Nose surgery that builds firm structural grafts from your own rib cartilage, used to rebuild or reshape the nose when septal or ear cartilage is not enough.

quick.overview:
Rib cartilage rhinoplasty rebuilds or reshapes the nose using cartilage taken from your own rib. People turn to it for major bridge reconstruction, revision surgery and extended grafts that give the nose firm support and a new shape.

Carved rib cartilage supplies large, sturdy grafts for the nasal bridge and tip support, which septal or ear cartilage often cannot provide. A retrospective cohort of 58 rib graft patients treated from 2000 to 2009 assessed graft stability, warping, revision and donor-site problems; the published evidence is made up of small surgeon case series.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon under anesthesia as part of a larger rhinoplasty, usually when septal cartilage is insufficient or a previous operation has used it up. The surgeon harvests rib cartilage through a chest incision, carves it into grafts such as a columellar strut or bridge graft, and builds them into the nose. The nose changes shape right away under swelling, and the final look settles as the swelling goes down over the following months.
quick.risks: The procedure adds a second surgical site on the chest, and studies track donor-site problems and graft warping. Rhinoplasty revision rates are roughly 5 to 20 percent overall. It is surgery with the general risks of anesthesia and rhinoplasty.

angle.text: Harvested rib cartilage is carved into large structural grafts that rebuild the bridge and tip, so the nose is visibly reshaped. Surgeons use it when septal cartilage is not enough, mainly for major reconstruction and revision rhinoplasty. Published results come from small surgeon series.

rhinoplasty-tip-narrowing-sutures.summary: Stitches placed in the nasal tip cartilage during rhinoplasty that narrow and refine a broad or bulbous tip without removing tissue.

quick.overview:
Tip-narrowing sutures give a broad or bulbous nasal tip a slimmer, more refined shape. The stitches reshape the cartilage rather than cutting it away, so the tip is narrowed while the tissue stays in place.

Sutures placed in the lower lateral cartilages pull and hold the folded cartilage in a tighter shape, narrowing the tip, and the change shows once swelling settles. General rhinoplasty references describe sutures as a standard way to narrow a wide tip; little published research has looked at the technique on its own.
quick.how: It is performed by a surgeon as one step within a rhinoplasty, often alongside other tip or bridge work. The nose is swollen at first, and the narrower tip becomes clear as healing progresses over the following months.
quick.risks: Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general, including revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. It is a surgical procedure performed under anesthesia.

angle.text: People with a broad or bulbous nasal tip get stitches that reshape and narrow the tip cartilage without removing it, giving a slimmer, more refined nose. The change is visible once healing is complete. Little dedicated research on the technique alone has been published.

deep-plane-facelift.summary: A facelift that lifts skin and the SMAS layer together as one unit after ligament release, tightening the jawline, midface and neck.

quick.overview:
A deep plane facelift tightens the jawline, lifts and fills the midface and smooths the neck by repositioning the skin and the underlying SMAS layer as a single unit. People choose it for a firmer lower face and fuller cheeks.

The surgeon releases the ligaments that hold the face in place, which lets the combined flap be moved to volumize the midface and jaw, with less reliance on skin tension. The evidence is mostly surgeon case series, technique papers and a few comparative studies; one study of 75 patients used objective apparent-age assessment after facial rejuvenation surgery including deep-plane facelift.
quick.how: It is performed by a surgeon under anesthesia, with incisions around the ear. Swelling and bruising come first, and the lifted jawline and midface show as it settles over the following weeks and months. It is sometimes combined with neck work or other facial procedures.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers) and scarring. Because the dissection lies close to facial nerve branches, it is considered technically demanding, and some surgeons regard sub-SMAS dissection as carrying a higher facial nerve risk. It is major surgery.

angle.text: Skin and SMAS are lifted together after ligament release, so the jawline looks tighter, the midface fuller and the neck smoother in one repositioned layer. The lift is visible once swelling resolves. Published results come mostly from surgeon series and technique papers.

smas-plication-facelift.summary: A less invasive facelift that folds and stitches the SMAS layer to give a moderate tightening of the cheeks, jowls and jawline.

quick.overview:
SMAS plication gives a moderate tightening of the lower face and jawline with less dissection than deep plane or SMAS flap facelifts. People choose it for firmer cheeks, jowls and neck line with a lighter operation.

The SMAS, the layer under the facial skin, is folded and stitched rather than cut and moved, and the skin is then redraped over the tighter foundation. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening with limited mobilization; the evidence is mainly surgeon series and comparative studies, including several comparing plication with deep-plane facelift.
quick.how: A surgeon performs it under anesthesia through incisions near the ear. Variants include short-scar versions and plication aimed at nasolabial folds or the platysma. Swelling and bruising settle over weeks, after which the firmer lower face shows.
quick.risks: Facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion. A meta-analysis found sub-SMAS techniques considered to have a higher complication profile than less invasive SMAS techniques. It is surgery.

angle.text: Folding and suturing the SMAS layer tightens the lower face and jawline moderately, with less mobilisation than deep plane or SMAS flap techniques. The firmer jowls and cheeks show once healed.

composite-facelift.summary: A deep facelift that lifts skin, SMAS and the eye-ring muscle together, raising the midface and smoothing the lower eyelid-to-cheek junction.

quick.overview:
The composite facelift lifts sagging cheeks and smooths the lower eyelid-to-cheek junction for a younger-looking midface and eye area. It reaches up into the periorbital region, which standard lower-face lifts do not usually do.

The skin, the SMAS and the orbicularis oculi muscle are raised and repositioned together as one flap, described as a modification of the deep-plane facelift. A 2008 surgical review describes pairing an upward-and-outward pull on the lower face with an upward-and-inward pull on the cheek and lower eyelid to balance the result. Published support is mainly surgeons' descriptions of their own technique and small series.
quick.how: It is performed by a licensed surgeon under anesthesia. Swelling and bruising settle over weeks, and the lifted cheek and eye area show as healing progresses. A 2008 review states that people with signs of a previous facelift, such as a lateral sweep or hollow eyes, may be corrected with it.
quick.risks: Documented complications of facelifts include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and skin necrosis, with smoking raising risk. Deeper planes bring the dissection closer to facial nerve branches. It is major surgery.

angle.text: Skin, SMAS and the orbicularis muscle are lifted as one layer to raise a sagging midface and smooth the lower eyelid-to-cheek junction, giving a younger cheek and eye area. The result is visible after healing. Evidence is at surgeon-series level.

subperiosteal-facelift.summary: A midface lift done beneath the periosteum, often endoscopically, that moves cheek tissue upward for fuller cheeks and softer nasolabial folds.

quick.overview:
The subperiosteal facelift raises sagging cheeks and softens deep nasolabial folds by repositioning the midface upward. People choose it for fuller, higher cheeks and a refreshed midface.

The surgeon frees the soft tissue from the facial bones by working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering bone, so the whole mask of the face can be moved as a unit and fixed higher. Surgeons described open and endoscopic versions in the 1990s; the endoscopic approach uses small incisions hidden in the hair. The available evidence is surgeon-reported series and anatomical studies.
quick.how: It is performed by a surgeon under anesthesia, either through small endoscopic incisions or an open approach, and is often combined with other techniques. A 1995 report describes the endoscopic procedure alone as suited to mild aging, and in men with alopecia in whom a coronal incision is a problem it may be combined with neck surgery. The lifted look appears once swelling resolves.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states the technique causes longer postoperative swelling than some alternatives. Anatomical studies highlight nerves in the cheekbone and temple region, such as the zygomaticotemporal nerve, whose injury can cause numbness or pain. General facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury and scarring.

angle.text: Lifting the midface tissue off the bone and fixing it higher raises sagging cheeks and softens deep nasolabial folds. The change is visible once swelling resolves, and it is documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.

mini-facelift-s-lift.summary: A short-scar facelift with small incisions near the ear that tightens early jowls and sagging with lighter recovery; Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.

quick.overview:
The mini facelift, or S-lift, tightens early jowling and modest sagging through shorter incisions around the ear and with less downtime than a traditional facelift. It is described as suiting people with deep nasolabial folds and sagging but a firm neck.

It suspends sagging tissue with a strong permanent purse-string suture and a short skin flap, with incisions in front of and below the ear shaped like an S. Surgeons describe less dramatic change than a full facelift, and Wikipedia describes the effect as more temporary. A 2007 review noted that studies comparing facelift methods are few.
quick.how: A surgeon performs it under anesthesia, usually without neck lifting. It may be combined with laser resurfacing, which has been reported in retrospective series. Recovery is shorter than for classic facelifts, and the tighter lower face shows as swelling settles.
quick.risks: Facelift risks in general include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and hair loss at incisions. Combining the S-lift with laser resurfacing has been reported in retrospective series, with side effect profiles described by the authors.

angle.text: Short incisions near the ear and a suspension suture tighten the lower face and jowls with lighter downtime than a full facelift. It suits sagging with a firm neck, and the change is visible after healing, though Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.

macs-lift.summary: A short-scar facelift that hangs the lower and mid face from above with purse-string sutures along a vertical vector, with quicker recovery reported by its surgeons.

quick.overview:
The MACS lift gives a firmer jawline and cheeks through a short incision in front of the ear and a purely vertical lift of the lower and middle face. People choose it for a quicker recovery than a classic facelift.

Permanent purse-string sutures anchored to firm tissue above suspend the sagging tissue upward with no lateral tension. It was proposed in 2002 as a modification of the S-lift. Its developers report operating times of about 2 to 2.5 hours under local anesthesia, and a quicker recovery with results they describe as comparably stable; independent assessments exist as well.
quick.how: A surgeon performs it, often under local anesthesia. The simple version uses two purse-string sutures for the neck and lower face, and the extended version adds a third, malar suture for the midface. Wikipedia gives a recovery of 2 to 3 weeks versus 3 to 4 for a traditional facelift.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says less skin is raised, so bleeding and nerve-injury risk are lower than with traditional facelifts, but general facelift risks still apply, including hematoma, scarring and nerve injury. Reviews have outlined limitations for the lower third of the face and the neck.

angle.text: Purse-string sutures suspend the lower and midface vertically from above, tightening the jawline and cheeks through a short scar with a quicker recovery. The lift is visible after healing; the recovery claims come from the authors' surgeon series.

aptos-thread-lift.summary: A non-surgical lift using barbed non-absorbable threads placed under the skin to hold sagging cheeks and jowls higher; case reports document migration and expulsion.

quick.overview:
APTOS threads lift sagging facial tissue without a surgical facelift. They are typically promoted for the cheeks, jowls and jawline as part of the broader thread-lift category.

Barbed polypropylene threads are inserted under the skin; the barbs grip the tissue and the thread is anchored so the tissue stays higher. Some authors describe a tissue response around the thread as well. An early report from the originator's group in 2002 described improved contour and lifting of various areas in a series of 186 patients; later literature includes case reports of complications and small retrospective studies of combined treatments.
quick.how: Threads are placed under the skin through small entry points in a short procedure, with no skin removal. A 2004 review describes short APTOS threads and long WOFFLES threads, with APTOS used for malar rounding and firming. A 2005 chapter describes the approach as the featherlift.
quick.risks: Reported problems include thread migration and partial expulsion; a MACS facelift has been used to correct APTOS complications. Wikipedia notes that UK practitioners face no mandatory qualification, cites a BBC investigation of short low-cost training courses, and quotes a physician describing thread lifts as potentially causing irreversible damage.

angle.text: Barbed threads placed under the skin anchor sagging cheek and jowl tissue in a higher position, improving contour without surgery. Early series, including 186 patients, reported better contour, while case reports describe thread migration and expulsion.

lower-facelift-with-neck-lift.summary: A combined jowl-and-neck lift that tightens deep facial layers and often adds platysma work and fat removal for a sharper jawline and neck line.

quick.overview:
A lower facelift with neck lift targets the jowls, jawline and neck together for a cleaner, sharper jaw-to-neck line. It typically tightens the deeper layers (the SMAS), may tighten the platysma muscle band, removes or contours fat under the chin, and trims and redrapes the skin.

Facelift tightening of SMAS or deep-plane tissue lifts the jowls, while platysma work, submental lipectomy and sometimes chin implants reshape the neck and under-chin contour. Published reports are mostly from surgeons describing their combined techniques; one 2018 team argues combinations of methods are essential for satisfactory lasting results. Registered trials include comparisons of office-based limited and hospital-based full facelifts.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon under anesthesia, with the mix of steps chosen to suit the person: liposuction, platysma tightening, fat pad removal, SMAS or deep-plane lifting and skin trimming. Swelling settles over weeks, and the jawline and neck definition shows as it resolves.
quick.risks: Documented facelift complications include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss; smoking raises the risk. Wikipedia notes the greater auricular nerve is the most frequently injured sensory nerve. It is major surgery.

angle.text: Tightening the SMAS and platysma and removing under-chin fat cleans up the jowls and neck so the jawline and neck line look sharper together. The result is visible after healing; the literature is surgeon-reported with limited comparative data.

skin-only-facelift.summary: The oldest and simplest facelift: lifting and trimming just the facial skin to tighten loose skin and mild jowls, with milder recovery and a shorter-lived result than deeper techniques.

quick.overview:
A skin-only facelift tightens loose facial skin and softens mild jowling by lifting the skin and removing the excess, without working on the SMAS or muscle beneath. It was the standard facelift for most of the early 20th century.

The surgeon raises a skin flap, pulls it in a chosen direction, trims the surplus and closes the incision, relying on the skin itself to hold the result. Encyclopedia summaries say it has fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper facelifts, and may suit a simple jowl lift in patients in their 30s and 40s, with results reported to last roughly 5 to 10 years. No dedicated trials were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon with incisions around the ear. Recovery is described as milder than for deeper facelifts, and the tighter skin shows once swelling settles. Some patients seek a touch-up sooner than others.
quick.risks: General facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and infection; smoking, hypertension and diabetes raise risk. The skin-only technique is described as having fewer complications than deeper variants, but excessive skin tension can distort the ears or give a windswept look.

angle.text: Lifting and trimming the facial skin tightens loose skin and softens mild jowls and sagging, with a milder recovery than deeper facelifts. The tightening is visible once healed. The surgical literature compares it with SMAS and deep-plane techniques, which are described as longer-lasting.

upper-blepharoplasty.summary: Removing excess upper-lid skin, muscle and fat through a crease incision to reduce hooding, so eyes look more open and rested.

quick.overview:
Upper blepharoplasty removes loose skin, muscle and sometimes fat from the upper eyelids so hooded or drooping lids lift and the eyes look more open and less tired. It is done both to clear skin that blocks vision and for cosmetic reasons.

The incision sits in the natural eyelid crease, so the scar is concealed. Published research includes technique papers, randomised comparisons of wound closure methods, a 2014 evidence-based review, and a study of how rejuvenation surgery affects how attractive, feminine and approachable faces are perceived.
quick.how: A surgeon marks an ellipse along the lid crease, removes the excess tissue and closes the incision with sutures or tissue glue. It is often paired with brow lifting or ptosis repair. Swelling and bruising last several weeks, after which the more open eye shows.
quick.risks: Swelling and bruising are common for several weeks. Dry eye and eyelid malposition are recognised concerns. Surgeons screen for dry eye, thyroid eye disease, bleeding disorders and body dysmorphic disorder beforehand, and registered studies are examining dry eye and vision changes after the operation.

angle.text: Excess upper-lid skin and fat are removed through a crease incision, so hooded lids lift and the eyes look more open and rested, with the scar hidden in the natural crease. The change is the surgical result itself. Evidence for appearance outcomes is mostly surgeon-reported.

fat-repositioning-tear-trough.summary: Lower-eyelid surgery that moves under-eye fat into the tear trough hollow instead of removing it, smoothing both bag and hollow.

quick.overview:
Fat repositioning softens under-eye bags and the tear trough hollow beneath them in one step, for a smoother, fresher lower lid. Rather than removing the bulging fat, as traditional lower blepharoplasty does, it relocates it.

Orbital fat that would otherwise form a bag is released and moved over the bony rim to fill the hollow below it. Published evidence consists of surgeon-reported case series of 66, 97 and 232 patients, covering transconjunctival repositioning, external fixation of the moved fat and whether visibly herniated fat is needed. No randomised trials were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: A surgeon performs it under anesthesia through an incision inside the lower lid or just under the lashes, sometimes securing the fat with fixation sutures. A canthopexy is sometimes added. The smoother lid contour shows after swelling settles.
quick.risks: Lower-eyelid surgery can cause eyelid malposition and other complications, and surgeons sometimes add a canthopexy to reduce that risk. Procedure-specific complication data were not summarised in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Under-eye fat is moved into the tear trough hollow rather than cut out, so the bag and the hollow smooth together for a fresher lower lid. The result is visible after healing. Support comes from surgeon case series rather than randomised trials.

co2-laser-blepharoplasty.summary: Eyelid surgery using a CO2 laser instead of a scalpel, with small studies reporting less bleeding and bruising and a similar final look.

quick.overview:
CO2 laser blepharoplasty gives the same eyelid reshaping as standard surgery, with a laser doing the cutting. People choose it for refreshed, smoother lids, and it can be paired with laser resurfacing of the fine wrinkles around the eyes.

The carbon dioxide laser vaporises tissue while sealing small blood vessels, giving a drier surgical field than a scalpel. Small side-by-side comparisons from the 1980s and 1990s report less bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, with no long-term difference in cosmetic result or scarring.
quick.how: A surgeon uses the laser in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery during upper or lower eyelid surgery, optionally adding resurfacing of the surrounding skin. Early recovery is described as easier with less bruising, and the final look is reported as similar to conventional technique.
quick.risks: General blepharoplasty risks apply. Published reports include a case of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty and cases of strabismus after cosmetic blepharoplasty.

angle.text: A CO2 laser takes the place of the scalpel to reshape eyelid skin and fat, sometimes with resurfacing of fine lines around the eyes. Small studies report less bleeding and bruising during recovery, with a similar final look.

double-eyelid-suture-non-incisional.summary: Stitch-only creation of an upper eyelid crease for larger, more defined eyes; fast and incision-free, though the crease can fade and buried sutures can irritate the eye.

quick.overview:
The non-incisional double eyelid method creates an upper-lid crease with buried stitches instead of a cut, giving larger, more defined eyes to people who lack a crease. It is a common East Asian aesthetic procedure and is described as quicker than the incisional approach.

Sutures passed through the lid bind the skin to deeper tissue such as the levator aponeurosis, so a fold forms when the eye opens. The new crease is visible straight away. Encyclopedia summaries say it is associated with fewer complications than the incisional approach but that the crease can be static and may fade. Published work is retrospective, including large cohorts on crease loss and reoperation.
quick.how: It is a short procedure done by a surgeon, with no skin removed. The crease shows immediately, with swelling settling over the following days to weeks. Some people have it redone if the crease loosens.
quick.risks: The crease may fade or loosen, requiring reoperation. Buried or exposed sutures can irritate or injure the cornea and have required removal. No randomised trials were found.

angle.text: Buried stitches bind the lid skin to deeper tissue to form an upper-lid crease without an incision, giving larger, more defined eyes in a quick procedure. The crease is visible straight away, and reports describe it sometimes fading over time.

le-fort-i-osteotomy.summary: Cutting and repositioning the upper jaw to correct bite and change midface projection and proportion; major surgery with a large clinical literature.

quick.overview:
A Le Fort I osteotomy cuts the upper jaw free and moves it up, forward or down, correcting bite problems and long-face deformity and changing midface projection and proportion. It is also used for cleft-related deficiency and as part of sleep apnoea surgery, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for reshaping the midface.

A horizontal bone cut above the tooth roots frees the maxilla, which is repositioned and fixed, usually with titanium plates and screws. The clinical literature is large but mostly observational, including a prospective evaluation of complications in 1000 patients and analyses of long-term stability by direction of movement; much of it concerns function rather than looks.
quick.how: It is performed by an oral and maxillofacial or craniofacial surgeon through the mouth under general anesthesia, usually planned with orthodontic care. Recovery involves weeks of restricted diet and months of bone healing, with the facial change showing as swelling settles.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, condylar resorption and, rarely, aseptic necrosis of the maxilla. In looksmaxxing forums there is sometimes disagreement about the aesthetic results. It is major jaw surgery.

angle.text: The upper jaw is cut and moved to a new position, which visibly changes midface projection and proportion along with the bite. It is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for reshaping the midface and has a large clinical literature, mostly on function.

t-osteotomy-genioplasty-mini-v-line.summary: Korean chin-bone surgery that narrows the chin toward a V-line and slightly lengthens it; described in surgeon technique reports and case series.

quick.overview:
The T-osteotomy, or mini V-line, narrows the chin toward a V-shaped lower face and, in many descriptions, lengthens it slightly. It is often discussed for people who feel the chin is wide relative to the jaw angle, and it originated in Korean craniofacial practice.

Through the mouth, the surgeon makes one horizontal and two vertical bone cuts, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece and refixes the segment with titanium plates, reattaching the mentalis muscle. A 2014 report in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery describes narrowing the front of the mandible, including the chin, while leaving the back of the jaw untouched. Evidence is surgeon technique reports and case series.
quick.how: It is performed by an oral and maxillofacial or plastic surgeon under anesthesia, and is discussed as an add-on in facial feminization surgery and as one option among jaw and chin procedures. Average lengthening of about 2-3 mm is described. The reshaped chin shows once swelling settles.
quick.risks: General genioplasty risks include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip numbness or weakness, and less commonly infection, bony changes and nerve damage. It is a surgical procedure.

angle.text: Trimming a trapezoid of chin bone and refixing the segment narrows the chin toward a V-line and, in many descriptions, lengthens it slightly. The new shape is visible once swelling settles. Support comes from surgeon technique reports and case series.

surgery-first-orthognathic-approach.summary: Corrective jaw surgery done before, or without, the long braces phase, so the facial change comes sooner; cohort studies report treatment-time findings that vary.

quick.overview:
Surgery-first reorders corrective jaw surgery so the bone operation comes before, or replaces, the traditional pre-surgical braces phase, which has typically lasted up to about a year. People choose it to see the change in jaw position and face shape sooner.

Surgeons using it cite 3D virtual planning and miniscrews for orthodontic control, which they say allow stable bite without pre-surgical tooth decompensation. The jaw is repositioned according to a virtual plan with a pre-set surgical bite, and orthodontic tooth movement follows afterwards. Studies, mostly cohort comparisons in skeletal class III patients, have looked at treatment time, stability, quality of life and planning accuracy, with a mix of findings including reduced total treatment time in some series.
quick.how: It is planned jointly by an orthodontist and a jaw surgeon: surgery first, then braces or aligners, often with miniscrew assistance, to finish the bite. Within looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as the route for people hoping for a faster change in facial structure.
quick.risks: Orthognathic surgery carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury with numbness that is usually temporary. A 2019 review discusses precautions and complications specific to the surgery-first sequence. It is major surgery.

angle.text: Doing jaw surgery first moves the jaws into their planned position sooner, so the facial change shows earlier and treatment can be shorter. The jaw repositioning itself is what changes face shape. Cohort studies report treatment-time and stability findings that vary.

custom-peek-jaw-implant.summary: A made-to-fit jaw implant in PEEK medical plastic for building up or reconstructing the jaw; the material is established in spine and skull surgery.

quick.overview:
A custom PEEK jaw implant is shaped to your anatomy to build up or reconstruct the jaw, giving a stronger, more defined jaw contour once healed. It is discussed as an alternative to other jaw implant materials.

PEEK (polyether ether ketone) is a rigid medical thermoplastic used in spinal fusion devices and as a partial skull replacement in neurosurgery. It is radiolucent, meaning largely transparent to X-rays, and because it is hydrophobic it may not fully fuse with bone. No clinical study of a custom PEEK implant for cosmetic jaw augmentation was found; registered studies involve PEEK in dental implant frameworks and facial plates.
quick.how: The implant is designed from a patient's scan and shaped to their anatomy, then placed against or fixed to the jawbone by a surgeon. The added contour shows once swelling settles.
quick.risks: No procedure-specific risk data were found. General implant surgery risks, such as infection and implant displacement, apply to facial implants as described for chin implants.

angle.text: A patient-specific PEEK implant is placed along the jaw to build up or reconstruct it, adding a more defined contour that is visible once healed. PEEK is established in spine and skull surgery; studies of cosmetic jaw use were not located.

maxillary-distraction-osteogenesis.summary: Gradual upper-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, used mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases and discussed for midface projection.

quick.overview:
Maxillary distraction osteogenesis advances a recessed upper jaw gradually, giving a more projected midface. It is used mainly for severe upper-jaw underdevelopment such as in cleft lip and palate, and in looksmaxxing contexts it is mentioned as a more extensive alternative to Le Fort I advancement.

The bone is cut and a distraction device is attached; the segments are slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap, rather than moving the jaw in one step. Early reports from the late 1990s described rigid external devices used in children and adolescents. Studies compare it with conventional advancement for relapse and stability, and a 2018 Cochrane review, as summarized by Wikipedia, found only one small study (47 participants) in cleft lip and palate, insufficient for general conclusions.
quick.how: After the cut, there is a latency of about a week, then activation at roughly 1 mm per day, and then a consolidation period lets the new bone mature before the device is removed. It has also been used in combination with mandibular distraction in hemifacial microsomia.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection, unintended direction of bone growth, hardware failure and, in craniofacial distraction generally, nerve injury. External devices carry pin-site infection and scarring risks. Cosmetic use in people without a deformity has not been studied.

angle.text: A bone-stretching device advances the cut upper jaw gradually, so the midface projects further and facial proportion changes. It is studied mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases rather than cosmetic use.
